reading.body:
CyrusOne SAT1 delivers 9 MW of IT capacity across 110,000 square feet, a density of 0.082 MW per thousand square feet that matches standard enterprise data centers rather than AI training campuses.

The Texas picture is mostly undisclosed. Of 133 mapped facilities in the state, only 14 percent publish a capacity figure, and the 475.41 MW total rests on those disclosures alone. SAT1's 9 MW ranks 14th among the 19 Texas sites that do publish, and accounts for 1.9 percent of the published state total. Rankings built on that sample describe who reports, not who is largest.

The certifications listed for SAT1, PCI DSS, HIPAA, FISMA, ISO 27001, SSAE 16 Type II and TIA-942, describe security and compliance posture. They say nothing about compute intensity or AI capability. The facility does not publish power density, cooling architecture, or GPU availability, so nothing here establishes whether it can host dense accelerator workloads. At a typical AI training density of 40 kW per rack, 9 MW would support roughly 225 racks, which is a small footprint by training campus standards.

What the data does not cover matters as much as what it does. There is no grid interconnection, no power source, no efficiency figure, and no announced expansion, which the suitability score of 56 flags as its missing input. Nameplate IT capacity is a ceiling on what a building can deliver to servers, not a measure of what it draws, and it is not a measure of what the grid must supply.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
